<div class="game-page">
<div class="game-head">
<div class="game-meta">game</div>
<div class="game-subtitle">Consisting of four variables and five back-games. (The 1790 edition prints this as the First Regular Party.)</div>
<hr class="game-rule">
</div>
<div class="philidor-game">
<div class="game-board">
<div class="pgn-board"><script type="text/pgn">[Event "Philidor, Analysis of the Game of Chess (London, 1777)"]
[Site "?"]
[Date "1777.??.??"]
[Round "-"]
[White "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Black "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Result "*"]
[Annotator "F. D. Philidor"]
[PhilidorGame "Method of Playing"]
[PhilidorKind "game"]
[SourceLine "5549"]

1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's
bishop's fourth square. (a) NOTE: This is the best place the king's bishop can occupy in the
first moves of a party. In that post he batters upon the adverse king's bishop's pawn, against
which the first attacks are generally formed.} Bc5 {The same. (b) NOTE: As the black may play
two other different ways, we will hereafter on that account make two different parties, under
the name of Variable.} 3. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} Qe7 {The queen, at her
king's second square. (c) NOTE: He hinders you from establishing two pawns in a front-line, and
occupying the centre. There are, on that move, three other ways of playing for the black; which
will be the subject of two variable, and one back-game.} 4. Nf3 {The king's knight, at his
bishop's third square. (d) NOTE: If you had moved this knight to your king's second square, you
would have lost the game. The subject of a back-game.} Nf6 {The same. (e) NOTE: Had he taken
your king's bishop's pawn, he would have played very ill. Another subject of a back-game.} 5.
Qe2 {The queen, at her king's second square.} d6 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 6. d3 {The
queen's pawn, one move. (g) NOTE: If you had pushed this pawn two moves, you would have occupied
the centre for a moment, but could not have kept it long, as will be seen by a back-game.} c6
{The queen's bishop's pawn, one move. (h) NOTE: If he had moved his queen's bishop to your
king's knight's fourth square, you should have pushed immediately your king's rook's pawn one
move. You must never leave your pieces restrained by the direction of the bishops, if you can
help it.} 7. h3 {The king's rook's pawn, one move.} h6 {The same. (i) NOTE: These pawns have
been mutually played to hinder the bishops from entangling the knights.} 8. Be3 {The queen's
bishop, at his king's third square. (k) NOTE: When your queen's pawn cannot break the direction
of the adverse king's bishop upon your king's bishop's pawn, you must preserve your queen's
bishop, in order to post him at your king's third square; because this bishop is the only piece
which can effectually be opposed to the adverse king's bishop.} Bxe3 {The king's bishop takes
the bishop. (l) NOTE: If he had moved his king's bishop, instead of taking your bishop, he would
have lost a turn: in the exchange of the pieces, it is always best to take the first.} 9. Qxe3
{The queen retakes the bishop.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square.} 10. Bxe6
{The king's bishop takes the bishop.} Qxe6 {The queen retakes the bishop. (m) NOTE: You may
conceive the advantage of your king's rook's pawn being pushed at the seventh move; for he might
now attack you with his king's knight, and afterwards push his king's bishop's pawn, to bring
him again into action. These precious moments must be carefully improved, especially in parties
wherein your adversary forces out your knights before your pawns.} 11. Nbd2 {The queen's knight,
at his queen's second square.} Nbd7 {The same.} 12. O-O {The king castles with his rook.} O-O
{The same. (n) NOTE: This game is quite equal; the white have preserved the advantage of the
move. He who first puts in motion his king's bishop's pawn, by pushing it two moves, will
undoubtedly have the advantage of situation.} *
</script></div>
